--- title: "The Bootstrap 👢" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # The Bootstrap

The empirical distribution and bootstrap samples

Bootstrap estimates of standard error and bias

Bootstrap confidence intervals: normal, basic, percentile, t, BCa

Application: cross-validation and model selection

::: notes - Rizzo Sections 8.1, 8.3-8.5. The jackknife (8.2) and jackknife-after-bootstrap (9.1) are in the next deck. - Data: law (LSAT/GPA, 15 law schools) and patch (8 subjects) from the bootstrap package, entered directly so the slides need no extra package. ::: ## Why the Bootstrap? - In Chapter 7 we simulated from a **known** model to study a procedure. - In practice, $F$ is **unknown**. The bootstrap (Efron, 1979) replaces $F$ with the **empirical distribution** $F_n$ and resamples the data. - "Pulling oneself up by one's bootstraps": estimating sampling variability from a **single** sample, without formulas and without replicate data sets. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Real world** $F\ \longrightarrow\ x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)\ \longrightarrow\ \hat\theta = s(x)$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Bootstrap world** $F_n\ \longrightarrow\ x^* = (x_1^*,\dots,x_n^*)\ \longrightarrow\ \hat\theta^* = s(x^*)$ ::: :::: ## Example 8.1: $F_n$ and Bootstrap Samples $x = \{2,2,1,1,5,4,4,3,1,2\}$: resampling selects 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with probabilities 0.3, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.1, i.e., the cdf of a bootstrap observation **is** $F_n$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(2, 2, 1, 1, 5, 4, 4, 3, 1, 2) table(x) / length(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x 1 2 3 4 5 0.3 0.3 0.1 0.2 0.1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) xstar <- replicate(10000, sample(x, replace = TRUE)) table(xstar) / length(xstar) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` xstar 1 2 3 4 5 0.30077 0.30114 0.09986 0.19853 0.09970 ``` ::: ::: ::: question How many distinct bootstrap samples of size $n$ are there? (Answer: $\binom{2n-1}{n}$; for $n = 15$ that is 77,558,760.) ::: ## Bootstrap Estimate of Standard Error ::: algo 1. For $b = 1,\dots,B$: draw $x^{*(b)}$ by sampling **with replacement** from $x$; compute $\hat\theta^{(b)} = s(x^{*(b)})$. 2. $\widehat{\se}_B(\hat\theta^*) = \sqrt{\dfrac1{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^B\big(\hat\theta^{(b)} - \bar{\hat\theta}^*\big)^2}$. ::: - $B = 50$ to $200$ is usually enough for an SE; confidence intervals need $B\ge 1000$. ## Example 8.2: SE of the Correlation (Law Data) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} B <- 200; n <- nrow(law); R <- numeric(B) set.seed(4750) for (b in 1:B) { i <- sample(1:n, size = n, replace = TRUE) # randomly select the indices LSAT <- law$LSAT[i]; GPA <- law$GPA[i] R[b] <- cor(LSAT, GPA) } c(theta.hat = cor(law$LSAT, law$GPA), se.R = sd(R)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` theta.hat se.R 0.7764 0.1332 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hist(R, prob = TRUE, breaks = 25, col = "#FFCC00", main = "Bootstrap replicates of r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/14-bootstrap/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Normal theory gives $\se(\hat\rho)\approx(1-\hat\rho^2)/\sqrt{n-3}$ = 0.115. ## Example 8.3: Using `boot()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} r <- function(x, i) { cor(x[i, 1], x[i, 2]) # want correlation of columns 1 and 2 } set.seed(4750) obj <- boot(data = law, statistic = r, R = 2000) obj ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ORDINARY NONPARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP Call: boot(data = law, statistic = r, R = 2000) Bootstrap Statistics : original bias std. error t1* 0.7764 -0.007608 0.1337 ``` ::: ::: - The statistic **must** take the data and an index vector `i` as its first two arguments. - `obj$t0` is $\hat\theta$; `obj$t` is the vector of $B$ replicates. ## Bootstrap Estimate of Bias $$ \bias(\hat\theta) = \E[\hat\theta] - \theta,\qquad \widehat{\bias}_B(\hat\theta) = \bar{\hat\theta}^* - \hat\theta. $$ **Example 8.4 (law data):** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} theta.hat <- cor(law$LSAT, law$GPA) c(bias = mean(obj$t) - theta.hat, se = sd(obj$t)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bias se -0.007608 0.133722 ``` ::: ::: - Rule of thumb: if $|\widehat\bias|/\widehat{\se} < 0.25$, bias correction is usually not worth it (it increases variance). ## Example 8.5: Bias of a Ratio Estimate (Patch Data) Eight subjects wore a placebo, an old, and a new hormone patch. Bioequivalence holds if $|\theta|\le 0.20$, where $$ \theta = \frac{\E(\text{new}) - \E(\text{old})}{\E(\text{old}) - \E(\text{placebo})},\qquad \hat\theta = \bar y/\bar z. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- nrow(patch); B <- 2000; theta.b <- numeric(B) theta.hat <- mean(patch$y) / mean(patch$z) set.seed(4750) for (b in 1:B) { i <- sample(1:n, size = n, replace = TRUE) theta.b[b] <- mean(patch$y[i]) / mean(patch$z[i]) } bias <- mean(theta.b) - theta.hat; se <- sd(theta.b) print(list(est = theta.hat, bias = bias, se = se, cv = bias / se)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $est [1] -0.07131 $bias [1] 0.008863 $se [1] 0.1018 $cv [1] 0.08708 ``` ::: ::: # Bootstrap Confidence Intervals ## Four Simple Intervals With replicates $\hat\theta^{(1)},\dots,\hat\theta^{(B)}$ and quantiles $\hat\theta^*_{q}$: - **Standard normal:** $\hat\theta\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\widehat{\se}(\hat\theta)$ (assumes $\hat\theta$ approximately normal, unbiased) - **Basic:** $\big(2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{1-\alpha/2},\ 2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{\alpha/2}\big)$ (pivot $\hat\theta - \theta$) - **Percentile:** $\big(\hat\theta^*_{\alpha/2},\ \hat\theta^*_{1-\alpha/2}\big)$ (transformation respecting) - **Bootstrap $t$:** $\big(\hat\theta - t^*_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{\se}(\hat\theta),\ \hat\theta - t^*_{\alpha/2}\widehat{\se}(\hat\theta)\big)$, with $t^{(b)} = (\hat\theta^{(b)} - \hat\theta)/\widehat{\se}(\hat\theta^{(b)})$ ## Why the Basic Interval Has That Form If the distribution of $\hat\theta - \theta$ is approximated by that of $\hat\theta^* - \hat\theta$: $$ 1-\alpha \approx P\big(\hat\theta^*_{\alpha/2} - \hat\theta \le \hat\theta - \theta \le \hat\theta^*_{1-\alpha/2} - \hat\theta\big) = P\big(2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{1-\alpha/2}\le\theta\le 2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{\alpha/2}\big). $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} alpha <- 0.05; th <- obj$t0; q <- quantile(obj$t, c(alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2), type = 1) rbind(normal = th + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) * sd(obj$t), basic = 2 * th - rev(q), percentile = q) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 97.5% 2.5% normal 0.5143 1.0385 basic 0.5937 1.0948 percentile 0.4580 0.9591 ``` ::: ::: ## Examples 8.9 - 8.10: `boot.ci()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} theta.boot <- function(dat, ind) mean(dat[ind, "y"]) / mean(dat[ind, "z"]) set.seed(4750) boot.patch <- boot(patch, statistic = theta.boot, R = 2000) boot.ci(boot.patch, type = c("basic", "norm", "perc")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` BOOTSTRAP CONFIDENCE INTERVAL CALCULATIONS Based on 2000 bootstrap replicates CALL : boot.ci(boot.out = boot.patch, type = c("basic", "norm", "perc")) Intervals : Level Normal Basic Percentile 95% (-0.2825, 0.1212 ) (-0.3108, 0.0923 ) (-0.2349, 0.1682 ) Calculations and Intervals on Original Scale ``` ::: ::: ::: question Is bioequivalence ($|\theta|\le 0.2$) supported by these intervals? ::: ## Visualizing the Intervals (Law Data) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ci <- boot.ci(obj, type = c("norm", "basic", "perc", "bca")) hist(obj$t, prob = TRUE, breaks = 40, col = "gray90", main = "Law data: bootstrap distribution of r", xlab = "r*") abline(v = obj$t0, lwd = 3) cols <- c("#2E5BBA", "#27AE60", "#C0392B", "#C2185B"); yy <- c(3.2, 2.7, 2.2, 1.7) segs <- rbind(ci$normal[2:3], ci$basic[4:5], ci$percent[4:5], ci$bca[4:5]) for (k in 1:4) segments(segs[k, 1], yy[k], segs[k, 2], yy[k], lwd = 6, col = cols[k]) legend("topleft", c("normal", "basic", "percentile", "BCa"), col = cols, lwd = 6, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/14-bootstrap/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: notes - The correlation is bounded by 1 and its distribution is skewed: the normal and basic intervals extend beyond 1 or misplace the skewness. ::: ## Example 8.11: The Bootstrap $t$ Interval Each replicate needs its own SE: a **bootstrap inside the bootstrap**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} boot.t.ci <- function(x, B = 500, R = 100, level = .95, statistic) { x <- as.matrix(x); n <- nrow(x) stat <- numeric(B); se <- numeric(B) boot.se <- function(x, R, f) { # local function to compute the bootstrap SE x <- as.matrix(x); m <- nrow(x) th <- replicate(R, expr = { i <- sample(1:m, size = m, replace = TRUE); f(x[i, ]) }) return(sd(th)) } for (b in 1:B) { j <- sample(1:n, size = n, replace = TRUE) y <- x[j, ] stat[b] <- statistic(y) se[b] <- boot.se(y, R = R, f = statistic) } stat0 <- statistic(x) t.stats <- (stat - stat0) / se se0 <- sd(stat) alpha <- 1 - level Qt <- quantile(t.stats, c(alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2), type = 1) names(Qt) <- rev(names(Qt)) rev(stat0 - Qt * se0) } ``` ::: ## Example 8.12: Bootstrap $t$ for the Patch Ratio ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- as.matrix(patch[, c("y", "z")]) stat <- function(dat) mean(dat[, 1]) / mean(dat[, 2]) set.seed(4750) ci <- boot.t.ci(dat, statistic = stat, B = 2000, R = 200) print(ci) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 97.5% -0.2504 0.4332 ``` ::: ::: - Cost: $B\times R = 400{,}000$ evaluations of the statistic. Second-order accurate, but can be erratic for small $n$ and is **not** transformation-respecting. ## Better Intervals: BCa **B**ias-**c**orrected and **a**ccelerated percentile interval: use adjusted percentiles $\hat\theta^*_{\alpha_1}, \hat\theta^*_{\alpha_2}$, $$ \alpha_1 = \Phi\!\left(\hat z_0 + \frac{\hat z_0 + z_{\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat a(\hat z_0 + z_{\alpha/2})}\right),\quad \alpha_2 = \Phi\!\left(\hat z_0 + \frac{\hat z_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat a(\hat z_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2})}\right), $$ - **Bias correction** $\hat z_0 = \Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac1B\sum_b I(\hat\theta^{(b)} < \hat\theta)\right)$ (median bias of $\hat\theta^*$) - **Acceleration** (from the jackknife, next lecture) $\hat a = \dfrac{\sum_i(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)} - \theta_{(i)})^3}{6\big[\sum_i(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)} - \theta_{(i)})^2\big]^{3/2}}$ ::: fact BCa is transformation respecting **and** second-order accurate. If $\hat z_0 = \hat a = 0$ it reduces to the percentile interval. ::: ## Examples 8.13 - 8.15: Computing BCa ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} boot.BCa <- function(x, th0, th, stat, conf = .95) { x <- as.matrix(x); n <- nrow(x); N <- 1:n alpha <- (1 + c(-conf, conf)) / 2; zalpha <- qnorm(alpha) z0 <- qnorm(sum(th < th0) / length(th)) # bias correction th.jack <- numeric(n) # acceleration via the jackknife for (i in 1:n) th.jack[i] <- stat(x, N[-i]) L <- mean(th.jack) - th.jack a <- sum(L^3) / (6 * sum(L^2)^1.5) adj.alpha <- pnorm(z0 + (z0 + zalpha) / (1 - a * (z0 + zalpha))) limits <- quantile(th, adj.alpha, type = 6) list("est" = th0, "BCa" = limits) } stat <- function(dat, index) mean(dat[index, 1]) / mean(dat[index, 2]) set.seed(4750) th <- replicate(2000, { i <- sample(1:8, 8, replace = TRUE); stat(dat, i) }) boot.BCa(dat, th0 = stat(dat, 1:8), th = th, stat = stat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $est [1] -0.07131 $BCa 3.284189% 98.17436% -0.2217 0.1865 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} boot.ci(boot.patch, type = "bca") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` BOOTSTRAP CONFIDENCE INTERVAL CALCULATIONS Based on 2000 bootstrap replicates CALL : boot.ci(boot.out = boot.patch, type = "bca") Intervals : Level BCa 95% (-0.2266, 0.1904 ) Calculations and Intervals on Original Scale ``` ::: ::: # Application: Cross-Validation ## Example 8.16: Model Selection (Iron Data) 53 measurements of iron content by a chemical and a magnetic method (`ironslag` in DAAG). Four candidate models: 1. Linear: $Y = \beta_0+\beta_1X+\varepsilon$ 2. Quadratic: $Y = \beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2X^2+\varepsilon$ 3. Exponential: $\log Y = \log\beta_0 + \beta_1X + \varepsilon$ 4. Log-log: $\log Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1\log X + \varepsilon$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} iron <- as.data.frame(matrix(scan("data/iron.dat", quiet = TRUE), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)) names(iron) <- c("chemical", "magnetic") chemical <- iron$chemical; magnetic <- iron$magnetic a <- seq(10, 40, .1) par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) L1 <- lm(magnetic ~ chemical); plot(chemical, magnetic, main = "Linear", pch = 16); lines(a, L1$coef[1] + L1$coef[2] * a, lwd = 2) L2 <- lm(magnetic ~ chemical + I(chemical^2)); plot(chemical, magnetic, main = "Quadratic", pch = 16) lines(a, L2$coef[1] + L2$coef[2] * a + L2$coef[3] * a^2, lwd = 2) L3 <- lm(log(magnetic) ~ chemical); plot(chemical, magnetic, main = "Exponential", pch = 16) lines(a, exp(L3$coef[1] + L3$coef[2] * a), lwd = 2) L4 <- lm(log(magnetic) ~ log(chemical)); plot(log(chemical), log(magnetic), main = "Log-Log", pch = 16) lines(log(a), L4$coef[1] + L4$coef[2] * log(a), lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/14-bootstrap/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 8.17: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- length(magnetic); e1 <- e2 <- e3 <- e4 <- numeric(n) for (k in 1:n) { # fit models on leave-one-out samples y <- magnetic[-k]; x <- chemical[-k] J1 <- lm(y ~ x); yhat1 <- J1$coef[1] + J1$coef[2] * chemical[k] e1[k] <- magnetic[k] - yhat1 J2 <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2)); yhat2 <- J2$coef[1] + J2$coef[2] * chemical[k] + J2$coef[3] * chemical[k]^2 e2[k] <- magnetic[k] - yhat2 J3 <- lm(log(y) ~ x); yhat3 <- exp(J3$coef[1] + J3$coef[2] * chemical[k]) e3[k] <- magnetic[k] - yhat3 J4 <- lm(log(y) ~ log(x)); yhat4 <- exp(J4$coef[1] + J4$coef[2] * log(chemical[k])) e4[k] <- magnetic[k] - yhat4 } c(linear = mean(e1^2), quadratic = mean(e2^2), exponential = mean(e3^2), loglog = mean(e4^2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` linear quadratic exponential loglog 19.56 17.85 18.44 20.45 ``` ::: ::: ::: tip The quadratic model has the smallest estimated prediction error. For linear smoothers, LOOCV has a shortcut: $\frac1n\sum\big(e_i/(1-h_{ii})\big)^2$ with leverages $h_{ii}$ (try `mean((resid(L2) / (1 - hatvalues(L2)))^2)`). ::: ## When Does the Bootstrap Fail? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); x <- runif(50, 0, 1) # theta = 1, theta.hat = max(x) bmax <- replicate(2000, max(sample(x, replace = TRUE))) c(P_star_equals_max = mean(bmax == max(x)), theory = 1 - (1 - 1 / 50)^50) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` P_star_equals_max theory 0.6200 0.6358 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hist(bmax, breaks = 40, col = "#FFCC00", main = "Bootstrap of the sample maximum: a spike at max(x)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/14-bootstrap/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - The bootstrap needs $\hat\theta$ to be a **smooth** functional of $F_n$; extremes, boundary parameters, and heavy tails break it. ## Summary ::: instructions - Bootstrap = plug in $F_n$ for $F$, resample with replacement, recompute. - SE: $B\approx 200$; bias: $\bar{\hat\theta}^* - \hat\theta$; intervals: $B\ge 1000$-$2000$. - Normal, basic, percentile, bootstrap $t$, BCa: prefer **BCa** (or bootstrap $t$) for skewed statistics. - `boot()` + `boot.ci()` do it all; write the statistic as `function(data, i)`. - Cross-validation estimates prediction error for model selection. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
